Random spatial tilings for spatially constrained null models

Source: R/tile_groups.R
tile_groups.Rd

Generates random groupings of sites by partitioning space into compact, equal-area tiles that are randomly positioned and oriented, independently for each column of the result. Passing the result as row_groups to nullcat_batch() or quantize_batch() randomizes each replicate within the tiles of its own tiling, so that sites only exchange values with nearby sites, and the resulting null distribution blends over many tile placements.

Usage

tile_groups(coords, spacing, n = 1L, lonlat = TRUE)

Arguments

coords

A two-column numeric matrix (or data frame) of site coordinates, one row per row of the community matrix. With lonlat = TRUE, longitude and latitude in decimal degrees; otherwise planar (projected) x and y coordinates.

spacing

The size of the tiles. With lonlat = FALSE, the distance between the centers of neighboring hexagonal tiles, in the units of coords. With lonlat = TRUE, the equivalent spacing in meters: tiles have the same area as hexagons with this center spacing (sqrt(3) / 2 * spacing^2), on a spherical Earth of radius 6,371,008.8 m. Either a single value, or a vector of length n giving the spacing for each tiling (e.g. random draws, for a blend of scales).

n

Number of tilings (columns of the result). Use one per randomization replicate.

lonlat

Logical: are coords longitude/latitude (TRUE, the default) or planar coordinates (FALSE)?

Value

An integer matrix with one row per site and n columns. Each column is one tiling, giving the tile membership of every site (tile labels are arbitrary and only meaningful within a column).

Details

Each tiling is built from a set of evenly spaced seed points, and every site is assigned to its nearest seed, so tiles are the Voronoi cells of the seeds.

With lonlat = FALSE, seeds form a regular hexagonal grid with a random rotation and offset for each tiling, so tiles are regular hexagons.

With lonlat = TRUE, seeds form a Fibonacci lattice on the sphere with a uniformly random 3-D rotation for each tiling. This works at any extent, up to the whole globe, with no projection distortion, and nearest seeds are found by a fast exact search, so fine spacings are no more costly than coarse ones. Tiles all have the same area, but not the same shape: the lattice is only approximately hexagonal, so depending on where sites fall on it, tiles range from irregular hexagons to near-squares.

Because tile placement is random, two sites a distance d apart share a tile in some tilings and not others. Since every tiling is placed and oriented at random, the probability that they share a tile depends only on d, not on where the sites are or the direction between them. It falls from 1 at d = 0 to about 0.5 at d = 0.42 * spacing and about 0.17 at d = 0.75 * spacing, and is near zero beyond d = spacing. It reaches zero at the tile diameter: 1.15 * spacing for regular hexagons, or about 1.3 * spacing on the sphere, where some tiles are slightly elongated. Otherwise the two give practically the same curve. This "co-tile" probability acts as the distance kernel of the null model: sites are pooled with their neighbors, and never with distant sites. Supplying a vector of spacings blends tiles of several sizes, which smooths and lengthens the kernel.

Sites near edges, gaps, or coastlines tend to fall in tiles with few other sites. A site alone in its tile cannot be changed by fixed-margin randomizations in that replicate. Use group_sizes() to check the average pool size of each site before running randomizations. When randomizing within groups, n_iter is applied to every tile; estimate it by passing the same groups to suggest_n_iter(), since tiles can need more or fewer iterations than the full matrix.

See also

group_sizes(), nullcat_batch(), quantize_batch()

Examples

# planar coordinates
set.seed(1)
xy <- cbind(runif(300, 0, 100), runif(300, 0, 100))
tiles <- tile_groups(xy, spacing = 30, n = 99, lonlat = FALSE)
summary(group_sizes(tiles))
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>   5.909  17.876  21.985  20.816  24.235  29.485 

# randomize a community matrix within a different tiling in each replicate
comm <- matrix(rbinom(300 * 20, 1, 0.3), 300)
sims <- nullcat_batch(comm, n_reps = 99, row_groups = tiles, n_iter = 500)

# geographic coordinates, with 200 km spacing
ll <- cbind(runif(300, -124, -114), runif(300, 32, 42))
tiles_ll <- tile_groups(ll, spacing = 200e3, n = 99)
